title: LEACH, HEED, PEGASIS, R-LEACH and ECH on the Intel Berkeley Lab's Measured Topology: A Transplant from Random Deployments to Real Positions and Measured Link Loss

study_type.label: Transplant
study_type.plain_meaning: Take a comparison the field always runs in one setting and run it, unchanged, in a more realistic setting, to see whether the result carries over.
study_type.mental_model: Like testing cars on a smooth test track and then on a real city road: same cars, same drivers, and you check whether the fastest car on the track is still fastest in town.
study_type.in_this_project: The comparison is five clustering protocols. The usual setting is a random layout with perfect links. The new setting is the real Intel Berkeley Lab deployment, reached in two steps: real positions first, then measured link loss.
study_type.how_to_explain_it: We are checking whether the ranking of sensor-network protocols that papers report on made-up random layouts still holds on a real deployment, and whether real positions or real link loss is behind any change.

elevator_pitch: Almost every paper on clustering protocols for sensor networks tests them on a random 100-node layout where every radio link works. We run five well-known protocols in one simulator on the same 52 sensors three ways: random positions, the real Intel Berkeley Lab positions, and those positions with the link loss measured there. Because each step changes one thing, we can say whether real geometry, real link loss, or neither changes the ranking.
overview: A wireless sensor network is a set of small battery-powered devices that measure something like temperature and send their readings over radio to a collection point, the sink. Batteries are rarely replaced, so how long the network keeps working depends on how carefully it spends energy. Clustering protocols save energy by letting a few nodes, the cluster heads, collect their neighbours' readings, combine them and pass them on.

Nearly every paper in this area tests its protocol on a random layout of 100 nodes, where every radio link works perfectly and energy depends only on distance. Recent surveys point out that this leaves an evaluation gap, because real deployments have fixed positions and lossy links.

In this project you build one shared Python simulator and rebuild five well-known protocols in it: LEACH, HEED, PEGASIS, R-LEACH and ECH. Each round, every alive sensor sends one 4000-bit packet, cluster heads combine them, and the result goes to the sink. You run the protocols on three versions of the same 52 sensors: random positions with perfect links, the real positions of the Intel Berkeley Lab deployment with perfect links, and those real positions where each transmission succeeds with the probability measured between those two motes, with up to eight attempts.

You then measure how long each protocol keeps the network alive and how many packets it delivers, and check whether the ranking changes at each step. If it holds, the field's usual setting is shown to be good enough for comparing these protocols. If it breaks, you can say whether real geometry or real link loss broke it.
why_it_matters: The study tests whether the protocol ranking the field reports on random, loss-free layouts still holds on a real measured deployment. Because the deployment changes one step at a time, it can also say whether real geometry or real link loss is behind any change in the ranking. If the ranking holds, the field's usual simulation setting is shown to be good enough for comparing these protocols, and if it breaks, reviewers learn which assumption misleads them. It tests whether the protocol ranking the field reports on random, loss-free layouts still holds on a real measured deployment that anyone can download, which is the evaluation gap recent surveys name.

research_questions.question: Does swapping random positions for the real Intel mote positions, with links still perfect, change which protocol keeps the network alive longest?
research_questions.already_known: The general point that simple radio assumptions can mislead protocol evaluation is established for MANET routing (Kotz et al. 2004). No study found by the novelty search runs these clustering protocols on the Intel measured topology (see 'What is already known').
research_questions.what_is_new: The geometry step on its own, with the node count, box and sink matched, and the Intel result set against 40 separate random topologies.
research_questions.deciding_number: For each of the 10 protocol pairs, the share of the 40 random-ideal topologies that agree with the intel-ideal winner (random_share), and whether it falls outside the 90% range (outside_90).

research_questions.question: On the same real positions, does adding the measured link loss reverse any pairwise result?
research_questions.already_known: Radio irregularity is known to hurt routing protocols more than MAC protocols (Zhou et al. 2004), and dense sensor links are known to be lossy (Zhao and Govindan 2003). The closest comparison of clustering protocols varies analytic energy models on synthetic layouts only (Kaushik et al. 2025).
research_questions.what_is_new: The link-loss step on its own, with measured per-pair delivery probabilities and a reversal counted only if it holds with both tuned parameter sets.
research_questions.answered_by: results/pairwise.csv at intel-ideal and at intel-measured with l1 and l3 parameters.
research_questions.deciding_number: Win rate and paired Wilcoxon p on the half-nodes-dead round for each of the 10 pairs, at intel-ideal against intel-measured with both parameter sets.

research_questions.question: Which protocols lose the most, in lifetime and in delivered packets per joule, once links are lossy, and which move up?
research_questions.already_known: Nothing found for this protocol set on measured links.
research_questions.what_is_new: Lifetime read beside packets delivered, PDR and packets per joule for each protocol at each level.
research_questions.deciding_number: Change in mean packets per joule and mean half-nodes-dead round per protocol from intel-ideal to intel-measured, with PDR at intel-measured.

research_questions.question: Does the shared simulator reproduce the published direction of the LEACH versus R-LEACH gap on the usual 100-node layout?
research_questions.already_known: The R-LEACH paper reports first node dead at round 1092 for LEACH and 1382 for R-LEACH, from one layout with no stated repetitions (R1).
research_questions.what_is_new: The same comparison over 40 seeds in a simulator shared by all five protocols. It checks the rebuilt LEACH and R-LEACH before the main grid is trusted.
research_questions.deciding_number: The sign and size of the mean first-node-dead gap between R-LEACH and LEACH over the 40 reference seeds.

prior_work.gap: We found no study that runs a set of classic clustering protocols on the Intel Berkeley Lab's measured connectivity, or that separates the effect of real positions from the effect of measured link loss for these protocols in one simulator.
prior_work.what_was_found: The closest hit is Kaushik et al. 2025 (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/271f93f2f067753a2c72969d1d7727f9d0e8820c). It compares LEACH with one other protocol under three analytic energy models (first-order, free-space, two-ray) with static and mobile sinks, on synthetic layouts and without measured links. Obi et al. 2025 (https://doi.org/10.26740/jistel.v2n1.p1-18) and a 2023 LEACH/PEGASIS/HEED comparison simulate synthetic layouts only. The general question, whether simple radio assumptions mislead protocol evaluation, was answered for MANET routing by Kotz et al. 2004 (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/4757d4c6a7371445768cdf91f795ad2b596bba73). Zhou et al. 2004 (https://doi.org/10.1145/990064.990081) showed radio irregularity hurts routing protocols more than MAC protocols, and Zhao and Govindan 2003 (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/2d87c72119d07f294f22fd4986bf0c8968e632d3) measured how lossy dense sensor links are. None of these runs clustering protocols such as LEACH, HEED, PEGASIS, R-LEACH or ECH on a real measured topology. Every query that named the Intel Lab data returned data-aggregation, prediction or anomaly-detection papers. So the novelty here is narrow. It is the transplant of this protocol set to this measured topology with the two realism steps separated. The general point that radio realism matters is already established. The verifier's later search also found a 2026 paper by Le Dirach, Boyer and Lochin showing that the choice of propagation model can reverse protocol rankings for ad hoc (MANET) routing. It is the nearest answer to the general question, but it covers neither WSN clustering protocols nor measured links.

reported_results.location: Section V and Table I, Section V.A text describing Fig. 6 (arXiv 1902.01445)

reported_results.says: Eelec 50 nJ/bit, threshold distance d0 87 m, 10 pJ/bit/m2 below d0, 0.0013 pJ/bit/m4 above it, EDA 5 nJ/bit. The largest distance between two Intel motes is 47.2 m, which is below d0.

contribution: It shows WSN routing researchers and reviewers whether the clustering-protocol ranking they rely on survives real positions and measured link loss on a public deployment, and which of the two causes any change.

key_terms.meaning: A set of small battery-powered devices (motes) that sense something like temperature and send their readings over radio to a collection point called the sink. Batteries are rarely replaced, so saving energy decides how long the network works.

A rule for grouping sensors so that a few of them, the cluster heads, collect their neighbours' readings, combine them and pass them on to the sink. Rotating the cluster-head role spreads the energy cost across nodes.
The node chosen in a round to receive its cluster members' packets, aggregate them and forward the result toward the sink. It spends more energy than an ordinary member in that round.

A simple energy formula for a radio. Sending a bit costs a fixed electronics energy plus an amplifier term that grows with the square of the distance, or with its fourth power beyond a crossover distance. Receiving a bit costs only the electronics energy.
Lifetime counted in rounds of data gathering. FND is the round when the first node runs out of energy, HND the round when half the nodes are dead, and LND the round when the last node dies.
The chance that one transmission from a given sender is received by a given receiver. Real radio links are often well below 100% and can differ in the two directions.
The share of the packets the sensors generate that actually reach the sink.

With ideal links every transmission arrives. With measured links each attempt arrives with the probability recorded for that pair of motes, so some packets need several attempts and some never arrive.

A significance test for two methods measured on the same set of cases, here the same random seeds. It ranks the per-case differences and asks whether one method wins more often and by more than chance would give.
The starting number for a random number generator. Fixing it makes a simulated layout and every random choice in a run repeat exactly, so two protocols can be compared on identical conditions.
One small sensor device in a deployment. The Intel Berkeley Lab deployment had 54 of them.
The collection point that all data is sent to. In this study it is mote 3 at (19.5, 19) at every level.
Combining several packets into one before sending it on. Cluster heads pay EDA = 5 nJ per bit to do it.

The distance where the radio model switches from the distance-squared term to the distance-to-the-fourth term. Here d0 = sqrt(efs/emp), about 87.7 m, which is longer than any distance in the Intel lab (47.2 m at most).
One try at sending a packet over a hop. At the measured-link level a hop gets up to 8 attempts, and each one costs transmit and receive energy.
The three levels of this study, each changing one thing: random-ideal, then intel-ideal (real positions), then intel-measured (real positions plus measured link loss).
Seeds 101-103 are used only to pick each protocol's parameter. Seeds 1-40 are used only for the reported results, like a test set.
For a pair of protocols, the share of the 40 paired seeds where the first one has the higher half-nodes-dead round.

concept_primers.intuition: Sending a bit costs a fixed amount for the electronics plus an amplifier cost that grows with distance squared. Receiving a bit costs only the electronics. Cluster heads also pay to combine packets.
concept_primers.example: One 4000-bit packet over 20 m costs 4000 x (50e-9 + 10e-12 x 400) = 0.000216 J to send and 4000 x 50e-9 = 0.0002 J to receive. The electronics part is most of it at this distance.
concept_primers.why_it_matters_here: Every protocol in the study pays from this one function. On the Intel layout no distance passes the 87.7 m crossover, so the distance-to-the-fourth branch never fires.
concept_primers.check_question: At 20 m, what share of the transmit cost comes from the distance term?

concept_primers.concept: What a measured link does to a packet
concept_primers.intuition: With ideal links every send arrives. With measured links each attempt arrives only with the probability recorded for that pair of motes, so the sender may try again, paying energy each time, and after 8 failures the packet is lost.
concept_primers.example: See the worked example 'What a weak link costs'.
concept_primers.why_it_matters_here: This is the only thing that changes between intel-ideal and intel-measured. Protocols with long hops meet more weak links.
concept_primers.check_question: Why can a protocol live longer at the measured-link level while doing a worse job?

concept_primers.intuition: If two things change between the runs you compare, you cannot tell which one caused the difference. The ladder changes positions in the first step and link loss in the second, and keeps everything else equal.
concept_primers.example: Fair: random-ideal and intel-ideal both use 52 sensors in the same 0.5-40.5 m by 1-31 m box with the sink at (19.5, 19). Unfair: comparing the usual 100-node, 100 x 100 m layout with the Intel layout, because node count, area and sink all change too.
concept_primers.why_it_matters_here: Every rule in 'Held fixed' exists to keep each step of the ladder to one change.
concept_primers.check_question: Why is mote 5 removed at all three levels, and not only at intel-measured?

concept_primers.concept: One real layout against forty random ones
concept_primers.intuition: The Intel lab is a single layout. Any single random layout can also reorder the protocols by luck. So the Intel result is compared with the spread of results across 40 separate random layouts.
concept_primers.example: See the worked example 'Is the Intel layout unusual?'.
concept_primers.why_it_matters_here: A geometry effect is claimed only when the Intel result lies outside what 90% of the 40 random topologies show.
concept_primers.check_question: If PEGASIS beats LEACH on 34 of the 40 random topologies, would losing to LEACH on the Intel layout count as a geometry effect?

concept_primers.intuition: Every protocol runs on the same 40 seeds, so you can compare two protocols seed by seed. The paired Wilcoxon test asks whether one wins more often, and by more, than chance would give.
concept_primers.example: If HEED has a higher half-nodes-dead round than ECH on 31 of the 40 seeds, its win rate over ECH is 31/40 = 0.775. The Wilcoxon test then checks the sizes of those 40 differences, not just their signs.
concept_primers.why_it_matters_here: With five protocols there are 10 pairs, and each is tested over 40 paired seeds. Five protocols are too few for a rank-correlation number to mean much.
concept_primers.check_question: Why is the comparison done pair by pair and not with one correlation between rankings?

concept_primers.intuition: A protocol's parameter is chosen on seeds that are never used for the results. If you tuned on the evaluation seeds, the choice would be fitted to the very runs you report.
concept_primers.example: LEACH's p is tried at 0.03, 0.05, 0.08 and 0.12 on seeds 101-103, and the value with the highest mean half-nodes-dead round is frozen in configs/tuned.json before seeds 1-40 are run.
concept_primers.why_it_matters_here: Tuning happens at both ends of the ladder, so a reversal at the measured-link level counts only if it shows up with both parameter sets.
concept_primers.check_question: What could go wrong if LEACH were tuned only at random-ideal and then run at intel-measured?

worked_examples.title: What a weak link costs
worked_examples.setup: Two hops of 20 m at the measured-link level, each allowed up to 8 attempts. Hop A has delivery probability 0.5, hop B has 0.1. One attempt costs 0.000216 J to send and 0.0002 J to receive, so 0.000416 J in total.
steps: Hop A: chance the packet arrives within 8 attempts = 1 - 0.5^8 = 0.996. Expected attempts = (1 - 0.5^8) / 0.5 = 1.99.
Hop A energy: 1.99 x 0.000416 J = about 0.00083 J, about twice the ideal-link cost of 0.000416 J.
Hop B: chance the packet arrives = 1 - 0.9^8 = 0.570. Expected attempts = (1 - 0.9^8) / 0.1 = 5.70.
Hop B energy: 5.70 x 0.000416 J = about 0.0024 J, about 5.7 times the ideal cost, and 43% of packets are still lost.
worked_examples.takeaway: A weak link burns energy on repeated attempts and still loses many packets. Protocols whose hops are long meet more such links.

worked_examples.title: Why lifetime alone can mislead
worked_examples.setup: Two protocols at intel-measured, each with 52 sensors at 0.5 J (26 J in total), run until all sensors are dead.
steps: PDR = packets delivered / packets generated: X = 30,000 / 50,000 = 0.60, Y = 40,500 / 45,000 = 0.90.
Packets per joule = packets delivered / energy spent: X = 30,000 / 26 = 1,154, Y = 40,500 / 26 = 1,558.
X lives 100 rounds longer by half-nodes-dead, but Y delivers 10,500 more packets from the same energy.
worked_examples.takeaway: At the measured-link level a protocol can stay alive longer by losing packets, so lifetime is always read beside packets delivered, PDR and packets per joule.

worked_examples.title: Is the Intel layout unusual?
worked_examples.setup: Two protocol pairs. For each, count on how many of the 40 random-ideal topologies the same protocol wins as on the intel-ideal level.

columns: random topologies with the same winner

steps: leach vs pegasis: only 3 of 40 random topologies agree with the Intel winner, which is under 10%. The Intel result lies outside what 90% of the random topologies show, so it counts as a geometry effect.
heed vs ech: 9 of 40 agree, which is over 10%. The Intel layout behaves like a typical random draw for this pair, so no geometry effect is claimed.
worked_examples.takeaway: A geometry effect needs the Intel result to be rare among single random layouts, not just different from their average.

methods.name: LEACH
methods.plain_description: The classic clustering protocol. Each round some sensors become cluster heads at random, the others join the nearest one, and each cluster head sends the combined data straight to the sink.
methods.key_idea: Rotating the cluster-head role at random spreads the energy cost over all sensors. Its long single hops from cluster head to sink are what may suffer most once links lose packets.
how_it_works: Each round, a sensor becomes a cluster head if a random draw falls below the threshold T(n) = p / (1 - p (r mod 1/p)), where p is the cluster-head fraction and r the round number.
Every other sensor joins the nearest cluster head.
Cluster heads aggregate their members' packets and send the result straight to the sink.
The cluster-head fraction p is the parameter this study tunes, over 0.03, 0.05, 0.08 and 0.12.

code.note: Your team writes it in the shared Python simulator. A third-party ns-3 module exists (wakwanza/leach, 53 stars, last push 2015-01-03, MIT), but it is not used because all five protocols must run in one simulator with one energy ledger. The R-LEACH paper restates the LEACH threshold as its Eq. 4.

paper.title: Energy-efficient communication protocol for wireless microsensor networks

gotchas: Use the threshold exactly as written in the paper and in R-LEACH's Eq. 4.
Members join the nearest cluster head by position only. They never look at the delivery probabilities.
It is tuned on held-out seeds over a 4-value grid at both the random-ideal and the intel-measured level.

methods.check_question: Why might LEACH's single long hops to the sink suffer most once links lose packets?

methods.name: HEED
methods.plain_description: A clustering protocol where sensors elect cluster heads over a few fixed rounds of messages, favouring nodes with more energy left.
methods.key_idea: Cluster heads are picked by remaining energy first and by how cheap it is to talk inside the cluster second, and the election always finishes in a small fixed number of iterations.
how_it_works: Each sensor starts with a probability of becoming a cluster head, set from its residual energy and the initial probability Cprob.
Over a small fixed number of iterations, sensors raise that probability and announce themselves as tentative or final cluster heads.
When there is a tie, the node with the lower intra-cluster communication cost wins.
Cluster heads then relay toward the sink over the cluster-head layer.
Cprob is the parameter this study tunes, over 0.02, 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2.

code.note: Your team rewrites it in Python from the paper's pseudocode. A MATLAB version sits in omarfarabi/Leach_Heed_Comparative_analysis (HEED_algo.m, 19 stars, last push 2019-09-15, no licence). You may read it, but it needs MATLAB, so it is not used.

methods.name: PEGASIS
methods.plain_description: A chain protocol. Sensors are linked into one chain of near neighbours, data is combined as it passes along the chain, and one leader per round sends it to the sink.
methods.key_idea: Short hops between neighbours replace long hops to a cluster head, so it may hold up better once long links lose packets.
how_it_works: A greedy chain is built starting from the node farthest from the sink, each time adding the nearest node not yet in the chain.
Data is fused as it passes along the chain.
A leader that rotates from round to round sends the fused data to the sink.
The chain is rebuilt whenever a node dies.

methods.name: R-LEACH
methods.plain_description: LEACH with one change: a sensor's chance of becoming cluster head is scaled by how much of its battery is left.
methods.key_idea: Nodes with more energy left take the cluster-head role more often. Its paper gives exact settings and published lifetimes, which makes it the reproduction check for the whole simulator.
how_it_works: It starts from the LEACH threshold T(n).
The threshold is multiplied by the node's residual energy over its initial energy (Eq. 5).
The optimal number of clusters comes from Eq. 6.
The settings in Table I are the ones copied for the 100-node reproduction.
The fraction p is tuned the same way as for LEACH.

methods.name: ECH (Enhanced Clustering Hierarchy)
methods.plain_description: A clustering protocol where sensors that sit close together take turns sleeping, so only the awake ones sense and send.
methods.key_idea: Its sleep rule depends on how close sensors are to each other, so it is the protocol most likely to react to the real mote layout.
how_it_works: Nodes that overlap or neighbour each other within an overlap radius take turns sleeping.
Only waking nodes sense and transmit in a round.
Cluster heads are drawn from nodes with higher remaining energy.
The overlap radius is the parameter this study tunes, over 2, 4, 6 and 8 m.

It is tuned on held-out seeds over a 4-value grid at both the random-ideal and the intel-measured level.

datasets.name: Intel Berkeley Research Lab sensor data (Intel Lab Data): connectivity.txt and mote_locs.txt
datasets.plain_description: Two small text files from a real 2004 deployment of 54 sensors in the Intel Berkeley Research Lab: where each mote sat on the floor, and how often a packet sent by one mote reached another.
datasets.role_in_study: The real deployment. Its positions make the intel-ideal level, and its measured delivery probabilities make the intel-measured level.
how_to_get: Open https://db.csail.mit.edu/labdata/labdata.html and click the connectivity and mote location links, or fetch https://db.csail.mit.edu/labdata/connectivity.txt and https://db.csail.mit.edu/labdata/mote_locs.txt with curl.
No account or form is involved. The large readings file data.txt.gz is not needed.
datasets.license_note: No SPDX licence. The page says: 'Permission is granted to use or reproduce this data in any format or venue, although we request that you acknowledge our hard efforts in any published work.' Cite the page and acknowledge Bodik, Hong, Guestrin, Madden, Paskin and Thibaux.
datasets.size: connectivity.txt is 82,677 bytes uncompressed (2,970 parseable rows plus one malformed '0 31' line; the server sends it gzip-encoded at about 29.7 KB), mote_locs.txt is 552 bytes (54 motes). The 34,422,518-byte readings file data.txt.gz is not needed.
datasets.image_format: Plain text. mote_locs.txt has one line per mote: mote id, x, y in metres. connectivity.txt has one line per directed pair: sender id, receiver id, delivery probability averaged over the whole 2004 deployment.
dataset_analysis: Plot the 54 mote positions (x 0.5-40.5 m, y 1-31 m) and draw the links above 0.5.
Make a table of mean delivery probability by 5 m distance bin. The idea's own check found about 0.52 under 5 m and about 0.04 between 20 and 50 m.
Count incoming links of probability at least 0.1 per mote, to pick the sink and see how lopsided the network is.
Check how asymmetric the links are by comparing the probability from A to B with B to A.
Find the motes that nobody hears (mote 5) and the ids with no coordinates (id 0), because both have to be dropped at every level.
known_issues: Line 2918 of connectivity.txt reads '0 31' with no probability. Skip and log it.
Id 0 appears only in connectivity.txt and has no coordinates.
Mote 5 has no non-zero outgoing link, so no mote ever hears it. It is dropped at all three levels.
No mote pair exceeds 0.90; the highest link probability in the file is 0.833, which the m500 log prints as 0.83.
The idea's text says 220 pairs exceed 0.5 and 458 are 0. The verifier found 220 only when id-0 rows are counted (187 among motes 1-54), and 457 off-diagonal zeros (511 with self-pairs).
Mote 3 at (19.5, 19) ties with motes 35 and 37 at 34 incoming links of at least 0.1. Break the tie by lowest id, which an argmax does by default, so the sink stays mote 3.
The probabilities are averaged over the whole deployment and were measured at the motes' fixed transmit power, so links that change over time are not represented.
The byte sizes the server reports (about 29.7 KB and 251 bytes) are gzip transfer sizes. Uncompressed the files are 82,677 and 552 bytes.

datasets.name: Synthetic random-deployment scenario under the Heinzelman first-order radio model
datasets.plain_description: Layouts your team generates: sensors scattered uniformly at random, with every radio link working perfectly. This is the setting most papers in the field use.
datasets.role_in_study: The random-ideal level (52 sensors in the Intel box with the sink at mote 3's position), the tuning layouts (seeds 101-103), and the separate 100-node reproduction check.
how_to_get: Nothing is downloaded. data/make_layouts.py generates one layout per seed from the parameters below.
Random52: 52 sensors uniform in x 0.5-40.5 m, y 1-31 m, sink at (19.5, 19), evaluation seeds 1-40 and tuning seeds 101-103.
Canonical100: 100 sensors uniform in a 100 x 100 m field, sink at (50, 50), seeds 1-40, used only for the reproduction check.
datasets.license_note: Not a downloaded dataset. The parameter conventions come from the LEACH paper and are restated in the R-LEACH (Table I) and PSO-ECSM (Table 5) papers.

Any single random layout can reorder the protocols by luck. That is why the study looks at all 40 random topologies one by one.

axis.name: deployment realism, changed one step at a time
axis.why: The first step swaps random positions for the real mote positions and keeps perfect links. The second step keeps the real positions and adds the measured link loss. So a ranking change between levels 1 and 2 can only come from geometry, and a change between levels 2 and 3 can only come from link loss.

levels.what_it_does: Places the 52 sensors uniformly at random in the 0.5-40.5 m by 1-31 m box, with the sink at (19.5, 19), and every transmission succeeds.
levels.keeps: the node count, box and sink of the Intel deployment
levels.throws_away: the real positions and the real link loss
levels.starting_settings: One layout per seed: evaluation seeds 1-40, tuning seeds 101-103.

levels.name: Intel positions, ideal links
levels.what_it_does: Uses the real coordinates of the 52 Intel motes with mote 3 as sink, and every transmission still succeeds.
levels.starting_settings: Positions from mote_locs.txt, with id 0 and mote 5 dropped.

levels.name: Intel positions, measured delivery probability
levels.what_it_does: Keeps the real positions and makes each attempt succeed with the probability measured between those two motes, with up to 8 attempts per hop.
levels.keeps: the real geometry and the averaged real link loss
levels.throws_away: how links changed over time, and the motes' fixed transmit power (the energy model still scales power with distance)

axis.settings_note: The protocols choose cluster heads, chains and routes from positions and energy only, at every level. They never see the delivery probabilities.

metrics.name: Rounds to first node dead, half nodes dead and last node dead (FND, HND, LND)
metrics.plain_meaning: The round when the first sensor runs out of energy, when half are dead, and when the last one dies.
metrics.why: These are the field's own lifetime measures, so the results can be set against published rankings. Reporting all three shows whether a protocol wins on stability or on tail lifetime.
metrics.used_for: The headline lifetime comparison at every level. Pairwise tests use the half-nodes-dead round.

metrics.name: Total packets delivered to the sink
metrics.plain_meaning: How many packets actually reached the sink over the whole run.
metrics.why: At level 3 a protocol can stay alive longer simply by losing packets, so lifetime alone would reward failure.

metrics.name: Packets delivered per joule spent
metrics.plain_meaning: Packets delivered divided by the energy spent.
metrics.why: It combines delivery and energy into one number that does not depend on when the run is stopped.

metrics.name: Packet delivery ratio (level 3)
metrics.plain_meaning: The share of generated packets that reached the sink.
metrics.why: It separates protocols that survive by sending less from protocols that survive by sending well.

metrics.name: Pairwise win rate across seeds with a paired Wilcoxon test
metrics.plain_meaning: For each of the 10 protocol pairs, the share of the 40 seeds one protocol wins, and a test of whether that win is more than chance.
metrics.why: Five protocols are too few for a rank-correlation statistic to mean much. Ten protocol pairs, each compared over 40 paired seeds, give a defensible test for each claimed reversal.

ml_task: Simulate periodic data gathering (one 4000-bit packet per alive sensor per round, aggregated at cluster heads and delivered to a sink) and measure network lifetime and packets delivered for each protocol at each deployment level.

experiment_design.how_runs_are_formed: There are four kinds of run, all in one shared simulator. Reproduction: 5 protocols x 40 seeds on the 100-node layout = 200 runs. Tuning: 4 tunable protocols x 2 levels x 4 parameter values x 3 seeds = 96 runs. Main round 1: 5 protocols x 2 ideal-link levels x 40 seeds = 400 runs. Main round 2: 5 protocols x 40 seeds at intel-measured with the random-ideal parameters (200 runs), plus 4 tunable protocols x 40 seeds with the intel-measured parameters (160 runs). That is 200 + 96 + 400 + 360 = 1,056 runs. The 15-run pilot in m700-protocols is extra and is covered by the pilot hours. Each row of the matrix below is one run.

factors.name: param_set
factors.note: tuned_l1 = value tuned at random-ideal, tuned_l3 = value tuned at intel-measured (intel-measured only), none = PEGASIS

factors.name: seed
factors.note: evaluation seeds. Tuning uses 101-103 and is never evaluated.

split.rule: Seeds are split once: tuning seeds 101-103 and evaluation seeds 1-40. Every protocol uses the same 40 evaluation seeds at every level.
split.why: If the tuning used the evaluation seeds, the chosen parameters would be fitted to the very runs that are reported.

how_each_part_is_used.evaluation: Seeds 1-40, used for every reported result and never looked at during tuning.
how_each_part_is_used.reproduction: Seeds 1-40 on the 100-node layout, used only to check LEACH and R-LEACH against the published numbers.

training_recipe.note: PEGASIS has no parameter, so it skips tuning. The 100-node reproduction uses the R-LEACH Table I parameters, recorded in configs/reference.json.

experiment_design.what_the_seed_changes: At random-ideal the seed picks the random layout and every random choice in the run. At the two Intel levels the layout is fixed, so the seed changes only the protocols' random choices and, at intel-measured, which attempts succeed. The same seed gives the same conditions to every protocol.
held_fixed: The same 52 sensors at every level. Mote 3 is the sink because it has the most incoming links with delivery probability of at least 0.1 (34 of them), and it sits at (19.5, 19). Mote 5 is dropped at every level because no mote ever hears it.
At level 1 the 52 sensors are placed uniformly at random in the same 0.5-40.5 m by 1-31 m box, with the sink at the same coordinates as mote 3.
Radio and energy constants: Eelec 50 nJ/bit, efs 10 pJ/bit/m2, emp 0.0013 pJ/bit/m4, EDA 5 nJ/bit, 0.5 J per sensor, 4000-bit data packets, one packet per alive sensor per round.
Protocols choose cluster heads, chains and routes from positions and energy only, as their papers describe. They never see the delivery probabilities.

At level 3 each attempt succeeds with the measured probability for that sender and receiver. A hop gets up to 8 attempts, and every attempt costs transmit and receive energy. Acknowledgements are not charged at any level.
The same 40 evaluation seeds for every protocol, and runs end when every sensor is dead or at 20,000 rounds.
One parameter-tuning procedure for every tunable protocol, run on 3 seeds that are never used for evaluation.

completed, or failed with the reason in the log.
Whether the run ended because every sensor died (all_dead) or at the 20,000-round cap (round_cap).
Read beside lifetime at the measured-link level.
The share of generated packets that arrived.

how_results_are_compared: For each level, compute the mean first, half and last node dead, packets delivered, packets per joule and (at intel-measured) PDR for every protocol.
For each of the 10 protocol pairs, compute the win rate over the 40 paired seeds and a paired Wilcoxon test on the half-nodes-dead round, at each level and at intel-measured with both parameter sets.
Rank the protocols on each of the 40 random-ideal topologies one at a time. A geometry effect is real only if a pairwise result at intel-ideal lies outside what 90% of those topologies show.
A link-loss effect is real only if a pairwise reversal between intel-ideal and intel-measured holds with both parameter sets.
The 100-node reproduction runs are compared only with the published R-LEACH numbers, never across levels.

confounds.confound: The Intel layout is one topology. Any single random layout can also reorder the protocols, so a ranking change at level 2 might be the luck of one draw.
confounds.plain_question: Is the Intel ranking different because real geometry matters, or because any one layout can shuffle the protocols?
confounds.if_ignored: One lucky or unlucky layout would be reported as a geometry effect.
confounds.how_it_is_handled: At level 1 the team records the ranking on each of the 40 random topologies separately. A geometry effect is claimed only when the Intel ranking (or a pairwise win) falls outside the range seen in at least 90% of those 40 per-topology rankings. Otherwise the paper reports that the Intel layout behaves like a typical random draw.

confounds.confound: Parameters tuned for random, loss-free layouts may suit some protocols better than others under link loss, so a reversal at level 3 could just be bad tuning.
confounds.plain_question: Did a protocol fall behind at the measured-link level only because its parameter was tuned for perfect links?
confounds.if_ignored: A tuning mismatch would be reported as a link-loss effect.
confounds.how_it_is_handled: Each tunable protocol is tuned twice, once at level 1 and once at level 3, on held-out seeds over a 4-value grid. Level 3 results are reported with both parameter sets, and a reversal counts only if it appears with both.

confounds.confound: The usual field setting (100 nodes in 100 x 100 m) differs from the Intel deployment in node count, area and sink position as well as in realism.
confounds.plain_question: Does the ranking change because of realism, or because the node count, area and sink moved too?
confounds.if_ignored: Differences in the setting would be credited to realism.
confounds.how_it_is_handled: Level 1 is built to match the Intel deployment in node count, bounding box and sink coordinates, so the ladder never mixes these in. The 100-node setting is run separately as a reproduction check and is not part of the comparison across levels.

confounds.confound: Published numbers for these protocols come from different simulators and energy bookkeeping, which can produce differences on their own.
confounds.plain_question: Do published numbers differ because the protocols differ, or because each paper used its own simulator and energy bookkeeping?
confounds.if_ignored: Simulator differences would be credited to the protocols.
confounds.how_it_is_handled: All five protocols run in one simulator with one energy function. A unit test checks the energy charged for a single packet against the first-order formula before any protocol code runs.

confounds.confound: Changing the node set between levels would move the result for reasons unrelated to realism. Mote 5 can never be heard at level 3.
confounds.plain_question: Did the result move because the set of sensors changed between levels?
confounds.if_ignored: A change in which motes are present would look like a realism effect.
confounds.how_it_is_handled: Mote 5 is removed at all three levels, so every level has the same 52 sensors and the same sink.

abstract: Nearly every clustering paper in this field tests its protocol on a random 100-node layout where every radio link works perfectly and energy depends only on distance. This study builds one shared Python simulator and runs five well-known clustering protocols (LEACH, HEED, PEGASIS, R-LEACH and ECH) on three deployments of the same 52 sensors. The first is the field's usual random layout with perfect links. The second uses the real mote positions from the Intel Berkeley Lab deployment, still with perfect links. The third keeps those real positions and makes each transmission succeed with the delivery probability measured between those two motes, with up to eight attempts. Because each step changes one thing, the team can say whether real geometry, real link loss, or neither changes which protocol keeps the network alive longest.

hypotheses.prediction: LEACH and R-LEACH, whose cluster heads send straight to the sink, lose the most lifetime and delivered packets per joule at level 3. Many long hops have delivery probability below 0.1 and need several attempts.
hypotheses.decided_by: Change in packets per joule and half-nodes-dead round from intel-ideal to intel-measured, per protocol, in results/summary_by_level.csv.
hypotheses.if_confirmed_means: Single long hops to the sink are what makes a clustering protocol fragile on lossy links.
hypotheses.if_refuted_means: Long direct hops are not the main weakness on this deployment. Look at which links the losing protocols actually used.

hypotheses.prediction: PEGASIS, whose chain hops are short, moves up the ranking at level 3.
hypotheses.decided_by: PEGASIS's pairwise win rates at intel-ideal against intel-measured, with both parameter sets.
hypotheses.if_confirmed_means: Short hops pay off once link loss is real, and the random, loss-free ranking understates chain protocols.
hypotheses.if_refuted_means: Chain hops alone do not protect PEGASIS from link loss on this deployment.

hypotheses.prediction: ECH changes most between levels 1 and 2, because its sleep-wake rule depends on how close the real motes are to each other.
hypotheses.decided_by: ECH's rows in results/geometry_test.csv and its change in mean half-nodes-dead round from random-ideal to intel-ideal.
hypotheses.if_confirmed_means: A density-based sleep rule is sensitive to real geometry, so random layouts can misjudge it.
hypotheses.if_refuted_means: The real mote layout behaves like a typical random draw for ECH.

hypotheses.prediction: R-LEACH beats LEACH on first node dead in the 100-node reproduction, in the same direction as the published 1092 versus 1382, but by a different margin.
hypotheses.decided_by: Mean first-node-dead gap between R-LEACH and LEACH in results/reference_summary.csv, compared with R1.
hypotheses.if_confirmed_means: The rebuilt LEACH and R-LEACH behave as published, so the main grid can be trusted.
hypotheses.if_refuted_means: Stop and recheck both implementations against the papers before the main grid.

null_result.what_it_is: The pairwise rankings are the same at all three levels within seed noise.
null_result.what_it_would_mean: The field's random, loss-free convention is good enough for ranking these protocols, even though absolute lifetimes change. That is publishable as evidence that the convention holds.

extensions.idea: Let cluster-head choice see link quality

compute.how_computed: Everything runs on the Colab CPU, and these hours are counted against the 60-hour envelope. Main grid: 5 protocols x 3 levels x 40 seeds = 600 runs. Level 3 with the level-3 tuned parameters: 4 tunable protocols x 40 seeds = 160 runs. Reproduction on 100 nodes: 5 x 40 = 200 runs. Tuning: 4 protocols x 2 levels x 4 values x 3 seeds = 96 runs. Total 600 + 160 + 200 + 96 = 1,056 runs. One run is up to about 3,000 rounds with 52 sensors at about 50 ms per round in numpy (HEED's election iterations and the level-3 retry draws are the slow parts), which is about 2.5 min. The 100-node runs are about twice as long, about 5 min. So (856 x 2.5 + 200 x 5) / 60 = (2,140 + 1,000) / 60 = 52.3 h, plus a 2-hour pilot, gives 54.3 h, an average of 3.1 min per run. No single run is above 10 minutes. Two worker processes on the two Colab cores halve the wall-clock time to about 26 h. Every run writes its own CSV to Drive, so a dead session loses at most one run. No GPU memory is used. Input files are 30 KB and all run outputs stay under 0.5 GB. 1,056 CPU runs plus a pilot come to 54.3 h on free Colab, no GPU, under 0.5 GB of disk, with per-run checkpoints to Drive. Intel Lab connectivity and location files are direct downloads with no login or form. The synthetic layouts are generated by the team.

risks.risk: The probabilities are averaged over the whole deployment, so links that vary over time are not tested.

reading_list.why: Origin of the PEGASIS chain arm.
reading_list.sections_to_read: The description of how the chain is built and how the leader rotates, and the simulation results against LEACH.
reading_list.what_to_remember: PEGASIS builds a greedy chain starting from the node farthest from the sink, fuses data along the chain, and lets nodes take turns sending to the sink. The abstract reports that it beats LEACH by about 100 to 300% when 1%, 20%, 50% and 100% of nodes die.
questions_to_ask: Why does PEGASIS have no parameter to tune in this study?
Why might short chain hops help PEGASIS once measured link loss is added?

reading_list.title: Residual Energy-Based Cluster-Head Selection in WSNs for IoT Application
reading_list.why: Origin of the R-LEACH arm, and the published numbers the reproduction check compares against.
reading_list.sections_to_read: Section V and Table I, and the Section V.A text describing Fig. 6 (in the free arXiv copy, 1902.01445). Also read Eq. 4, Eq. 5 and Eq. 6.
reading_list.what_to_remember: The simulations use 100 nodes deployed randomly with the base station at the centre, 0.5 J per node and 4000-bit packets. The first node dies at round 1092 for LEACH and 1382 for R-LEACH, and the last node at 1510 and 2474. The text gives no number of repetitions or seeds. R-LEACH multiplies the LEACH threshold by residual over initial energy (Eq. 5) and sets the cluster count from Eq. 6.
questions_to_ask: Why does the study expect the same direction as 1092 versus 1382 but not the same numbers?
What does it mean for the results that the paper reports one layout with no stated repetitions?
Which Table I parameters does the reproduction step copy?

reading_list.title: ECH: An Enhanced Clustering Hierarchy Approach to Maximize Lifetime of Wireless Sensor Networks
reading_list.why: Origin of the ECH arm and its sleep-wake rule for overlapping nodes.
reading_list.sections_to_read: The description of the sleeping-waking mechanism for overlapping and neighbouring nodes and of cluster-head selection.
reading_list.what_to_remember: ECH lets overlapping and neighbouring nodes sleep in turns so only waking nodes collect and send data, and it picks cluster heads from nodes with higher remaining energy. Write down the exact sleep-wake rule. The overlap radius is the parameter this study tunes.
questions_to_ask: Why would a density-based sleep rule react to the real Intel mote layout more than the other protocols?
How does the overlap radius decide which nodes sleep?

reading_list.title: Low energy adaptive clustering hierarchy with deterministic cluster-head selection
reading_list.why: Origin of the first-node-dead, half-nodes-dead and last-node-dead lifetime metrics used here.
reading_list.sections_to_read: The section that defines the lifetime metrics.
reading_list.what_to_remember: The paper adds a deterministic part to LEACH's cluster-head selection and introduces three lifetime metrics: First Node Dies, Half of the Nodes Alive and Last Node Dies. This study reports all three.
questions_to_ask: Why report all three lifetime metrics and not only the first node dead?
Why can lifetime alone be misleading at the measured-link level, and which metric corrects for it?

reading_list.title: Performance Analysis of Cluster-Based Routing Protocols under Propagation and Mobility Variants in Wireless Sensor Networks
reading_list.why: Closest prior comparison: cluster protocols under several analytic energy models, which this study goes beyond with measured links.
reading_list.sections_to_read: The description of the energy models and sink scenarios, and the results for first and last node dead.
reading_list.what_to_remember: This is the closest earlier comparison. It compares LEACH with DCREA under the first-order, free-space and two-ray energy models, with static and mobile sinks, on synthetic layouts and without measured links. Write down which energy models it varies and what it does not test.
questions_to_ask: How is varying analytic energy models different from adding measured link loss?
What would this study add even if its ranking matched the one in this paper?

reading_list.title: Experimental evaluation of wireless simulation assumptions
reading_list.why: Shows for MANET routing that simple radio assumptions can mislead an evaluation, the general case of this study's question.
reading_list.sections_to_read: The list of simple radio assumptions it tests and the comparison of simulated with measured results.
reading_list.what_to_remember: It showed for MANET routing that simple radio assumptions can mislead a protocol evaluation, which is the general version of this study's question. Note which assumptions it found most misleading.
questions_to_ask: Which of the assumptions this paper tests does the measured-link level remove?
Why is the general point already established, and what is new about this study?

reading_list.title: Impact of radio irregularity on wireless sensor networks
reading_list.why: Shows that radio irregularity affects routing protocols, which motivates the measured-link level.
reading_list.sections_to_read: The description of the Radio Irregularity Model and the results on MAC and routing protocols.
reading_list.what_to_remember: Using MICA2 measurements, the authors built the Radio Irregularity Model and found that radio irregularity has a significant impact on routing protocols but a relatively small one on MAC protocols.
questions_to_ask: Why does this finding suggest clustering protocols may react to measured link loss?
How is a measured delivery probability per mote pair different from a radio irregularity model?

reading_list.title: Understanding packet delivery performance in dense wireless sensor networks
reading_list.why: Measures packet delivery in dense sensor networks and explains why links like Intel's are lossy and asymmetric.
reading_list.sections_to_read: The measurements of packet delivery against distance and the discussion of asymmetric links.
reading_list.what_to_remember: It measured how lossy and asymmetric links are in dense sensor networks. Note how delivery changes with distance, so you can set it beside the Intel numbers: a mean probability of 0.52 under 5 m and 0.04 between 20 and 50 m.
questions_to_ask: Why are links in a dense indoor deployment like Intel's asymmetric?
What does a link with delivery probability below 0.1 cost a protocol that needs up to 8 attempts?

reading_list.title: Link-Quality-Based Energy-Efficient Routing Protocol for WSN in IoT
reading_list.why: One of the few routing papers that models link quality explicitly, which gives a point of comparison for the level-3 results.
reading_list.sections_to_read: The description of how LQEER estimates link quality and uses it in route choice, and the results on packet delivery ratio.
reading_list.what_to_remember: LQEER uses link-quality estimation together with energy to choose routes, and the authors report better packet delivery ratio, energy consumption and delay than the protocols they compare against. It is a point of comparison for the measured-link results.
questions_to_ask: Why do the five protocols in this study never see the delivery probabilities, while LQEER uses link quality?
What would the measured-link results suggest about adding link quality to cluster-head choice?

milestones.title: Build the shared round-based simulator and energy ledger
pre_brief: Why is the energy function tested before any protocol code exists?
With a delivery probability of 0.5 and up to 8 attempts, about how many attempts does one packet take on average?
milestones.instructions: Write sim/core.py. It holds node state (position, residual energy, alive flag), a round loop, and one function radio_cost(bits, distance) that applies the first-order model with Eelec 50 nJ/bit, efs 10 pJ/bit/m2, emp 0.0013 pJ/bit/m4 and the crossover at sqrt(efs/emp), about 87.7 m. Add EDA 5 nJ/bit for aggregation at cluster heads. Every sensor starts with 0.5 J and sends one 4000-bit packet per round while alive. Add a link layer with two modes. In ideal mode every attempt succeeds. In measured mode each attempt succeeds with the matrix probability for that sender and receiver, up to 8 attempts, and each attempt charges transmit energy to the sender and receive energy to the receiver. Acknowledgements are not charged in either mode. Log one row per round with alive count, energy spent, packets generated and packets delivered. Stop a run when every sensor is dead or at 20,000 rounds, and save each run as one CSV plus one JSON config. Write tests/test_energy.py. It checks that one 4000-bit packet over 20 m costs exactly 4000 x (50e-9 + 10e-12 x 400) J to transmit, and that a probability of 0.5 gives about 2 attempts on average over 10,000 draws. This test runs before any protocol code exists, so that all five protocols later share one checked energy function. Published numbers for these protocols come from different simulators with different energy bookkeeping, and this is what keeps that difference out of your comparison. This goes into the experimental setup section.

milestones.title: Implement LEACH, HEED, PEGASIS, R-LEACH and ECH in the simulator
pre_brief: Why may no protocol read the delivery probabilities?
When a paper leaves a detail unstated, where does your choice get written down, and why does that choice have to stay the same at every level?
milestones.instructions: All five protocols are rebuilt by your team, because they must run in one simulator with one energy ledger. Write one file per protocol in sim/protocols/. Each exposes setup_round(state, rng) and route(state), which return the cluster heads or chain and the next hop for every packet, using only positions and energies. No protocol may read the delivery probabilities. Build each from what its paper gives you, using your notes from milestone 2. LEACH uses the threshold T(n) = p / (1 - p (r mod 1/p)). Members join the nearest cluster head and cluster heads send straight to the sink. R-LEACH: the same threshold multiplied by residual over initial energy (Eq. 5), with the cluster count from Eq. 6 and the settings in Table I. HEED: the iteration pseudocode in the paper. A MATLAB version exists in omarfarabi/Leach_Heed_Comparative_analysis (HEED_algo.m), which you may read but must rewrite in Python. PEGASIS: a greedy chain built from the node farthest from the sink, data fused along it, a rotating leader, and the chain rebuilt whenever a node dies. ECH: the sleep-wake rule for overlapping and neighbouring nodes, with cluster heads drawn from nodes with more energy left. Where a paper leaves a detail unstated, choose the simplest reading, write it in docs/protocol_choices.md with the page you were reading, and use that choice at every level. Test each protocol on a 10-node toy layout where you can check the cluster heads by hand. That hand check is the first test that a rebuilt protocol works. The second is the reproduction in milestone 7, and no protocol enters the main comparison until both pass. Then run a small pilot end to end: every protocol on seed 1 at all three levels (15 runs). Check that alive nodes fall over time and no energy goes negative, and time the milliseconds per round. The compute plan assumes about 50 ms per round. If rounds are slower than 60 ms, the plan is to cut the 100-node reproduction runs to 20 seeds before anything in the main grid is cut, and you record that decision here. This goes into the methods section.
